newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto dodges ASEAN traffic jams.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto dodges ASEAN traffic jams.

text.p: Indonesia's President Suharto, whose motorcades get special clearance through Jakarta's clogged streets, turned up for Saturday's ASEAN summit an hour early to avoid causing a traffic jam.
Commuters in the city of some 10 million are inured to traffic chaos, but they were left swearing on Friday as leaders of 10 Southeast Asian nations gathered for the meeting.
Indonesia, Philippines, Brunei, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore are full ASEAN members, with Laos, Cambodia and Burma attending as observers.
Traffic took hours to untangle after motorcades swept between the luxury hotel where the leaders stayed in the heart of the business district and the state palace.
Suharto arrived an hour early for the summit. "He wanted to avoid another traffic jam," a foreign ministry official said.
Even a one-day ASEAN summit couldn't keep Philippine President Fidel Ramos away from the golf links.

ASEAN leaders normally fit in a round of golf at their meetings, but the brief summit in Jakarta kept most of them tied to their chairs. Indonesia's President Suharto gave up his usual Saturday round as host leader.
Ramos, however, managed to slip out for a quick game shortly after arriving on Friday and did not return until late in the evening, officials said.

ASEAN leaders switched to Indonesian batik shirts for the "informal" summit. The loose, long-sleeved silk shirts in gold and brown patterns worn outside the trousers are Indonesia's equivalent of formal wear.
Many of the same leaders wore barong tagalog shirts, the Philippines national dress, during the recent Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meeting in Manila.
As is usual when Indonesian President Suharto is present, journalists covering the ASEAN summit were told to wear collars and ties. Jeans were banned.

While ASEAN leaders met at a luxury hotel on Saturday morning, the four leaders from observer nations Laos, Cambodia (with a first and second prime minister) and Burma were briefed at ASEAN headquarters.

They "surfed" the ASEAN homepage on the Internet (www.aseansec.org), but ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh diplomatically avoided the section on the group's last ministerial meeting in Jakarta in July.
"I don't think we need to go into that," he told them. The July meeting was embroiled in controversy over Burma's inclusion in ASEAN.
